newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: South Pacific nations seek economy reform blueprint.
newsitem.headline: South Pacific nations seek economy reform blueprint.

text.p: Leading South Pacific countries will seek a strategy to turn around the flagging economies of Pacific island nations and reduce their dependence on aid when key ministers meet in this tropical Australian resort town on Friday.
Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said the countries could not survive with continued high deficits and bloated public sectors.
Costello is hosting the inaugural summit of economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific Foroum. Forum leaders set up the summit in a bid to speed economic reforms and lift living standards.
"Where countries run very large public sectors, very large budget deficits -- it's hard to do that on a sustainable basis," he told reporters on the eve of the summit.

"We'll be encouraging our neighbours to adopt more prudent fiscal policies. The economic aim of the conference is to try to encourage all members of the forum to get to a position where they have sustainable economic outlooks."
The forum's two largest members, Australia and New Zealand, have economies that dwarf those of other members.
Foreign aid, particularly from Australia, New Zealand and the United States, plays a key role in supporting living standards.
Forum officials hope Friday's meeting can agree on an economic action plan cutting tariffs, liberalising investment policies and increasing the transparency of budget policies and decisions.
"They have been asked by their leaders to do a job -- therefore we are hoping that reasonably solid issues come from this," forum deputy secretary-general Tony Slatyer told reporters.
"... issues of tariff reform and investment policy reform and public sector reform are pretty fundamental to the island countries."

In addition to Australia and New Zealand, the remaining members -- all island countries with small populations -- are the Cook Islands, Fiji, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Nauru, Niue, Papua New Guinea, Palau, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

The 14 island countries have economies marked by low growth, surging imports, high debt, bloated public sectors and weak private sectors, a foreign aid accounting for up to 70 percent of their gross domestic product.
Exports are largely resources, fishing rights and tourism.

Some have begun basic economic reforms, but forum leaders acknowledged at their last summit, in September 1996, that they needed to speed the pace of change to boost their economic strength and encourage foreign investment.
